Baddeleyite Pb Pb geochronology and paleomagnetic poles for
~1.89–1.86 Ga mafic intrusions from the Dharwar craton, India, and their
paleogeographic implications
V. Parashuramulu, Ravi Shankar, D. Srinivasa Sarma*, E. Nagaraju, N. Ramesh Babu
CSIR-National Geophysical Research Institute, Council of Scientific and Industrial Research, Uppal Road, Hyderabad 500 007, India
A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T
Keywords: We present new key paleomagnetic pole at 13◦S, 152◦E (k =21, A95 =7.8◦) for recently identified 1864.4 ±2.7
Mafic dykes Ma (weighted mean age of four Pb–Pb ages) mafic magmatic event, based on a detailed paleomagnetic study of
Dharwar craton dolerite dykes and sills intruding Archean basement rocks and Tadipatri formation of the Cuddapah basin,
Baddeleyite geochronology Dharwar craton respectively. The Pb–Pb baddeleyite geochronology yields a crystallisation age of 1867.1 ±1.0
Paleomagnetism Ma (MSWD =1.02) for N77◦E trending dyke in the southern region to Cuddapah basin. This new age obtained,
Large Igneous Province
confirms the presence of ~1864 Ma magmatic episode with a spatial extent of ~400 km in the Eastern Dharwar
Supercontinent
craton, within the brief period of ~5 Ma. The paleomagnetic results in these dykes revealed reverse polarity
magnetisation direction with mean D =107◦, I =24◦(N =13 sites, α 95 =10◦). Here, we also update the normal
polarity magnetic directions on ~1.89 Ga swarm, and the corresponding paleopole situated at 21◦N, 336◦E (N =
79 sites, A95 =3.6◦). The paleoposition of India is constrained around the equator during ~1.89–1.86 Ga time.
The paleogeographic reconstructions were also been attempted at ~1.89 Ga and ~ 1.86 Ga with available key
poles from other cratons, indicates the possibility of single plume acting as a source for two distinguishable radial
emplacement of mafic dyke swarms across India (Dharwar and Bastar craton) and Western Australia (Yilgarn
craton) within a time span of ~35 Ma. The individual movement of India, Baltica and Siberia with a drift rate of
~5.55 cm/yr towards the south, whereas Amazonia craton has moved rapidly to the north (~24.9 cm/yr), do not
suggest the amalgamation of a supercontinent (Columbia/ Nuna) during ~1.88–1.86 Ga time.

4.2. Paleomagnetic studies
A total of 259 specimens (combining dykes and sills samples) from
26 sites (minimum four specimens per site) were subjected to standard
alternating field demagnetisation (AF) using Molspin Alternating Field
demagnetiser and thermal (TH) demagnetisation using MMTD 80 oven

5.4.2. 1864 Ma swarm
Altogether 65 specimens from seven sites, including three mafic
dykes (35 specimens) and sills (at 3 sites, 30 specimens) of ~1864 Ma
swarm are presented here. Most of these samples show consistent NRM
intensities for all the dykes and sills. High blocking temperature (TH)
and high coercivity (AF) nature of component reveal stable magnetic
directions (Fig. 7) with a south-easterly declination and shallow incli-
nation (Fig. 6). These directions exhibit reversed polarity magnetisation
relative to ~1886 Ma directions. However, within site mean directions
of all seven sites of this event yielded a mean of declination = 101◦,
inclination =28◦(k =76, α 95 =8◦) with a corresponding paleopole at
6◦S, 152◦E (dp =5◦, dm =9◦).
Similar magnetic remanence directions have been reported earlier
from several mafic intrusions adjacent to Cuddapah basin (Radhak-
rishna et al., 2013b; Belica et al., 2014). Such results are given in
Table 2, and locations are shown in Fig. 9. Combined paleomagnetic
direction from the present study together with the previously reported
data gave a mean declination =107◦, inclination =24◦, (k =21, α 95 =

acteristic remanence directions with ovals of 95% confidence from the ~1886 =10 ◦ ) (Fig. 8).

euler rotation parameters (to the absolute framework) used in these reconstructions are given in Table 3. The pole and craton/continent pairs are depicted by same
colour combination. The mafic dykes and related coeval magmatism in all cratons are shown by red colour. The black arrows demonstrate the present day North for
individual cratons/continents. (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.)
